content.body: Have you ever wondered how to find all the anagrams of a word hidden inside a longer text? This is a common pattern matching challenge. Today we'll learn an efficient way to solve it using a clever memory technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain what an anagram is in the context of string comparison.
2. Apply a frequency counting technique using objects to track character counts.
3. Implement a sliding window approach to find all anagram starting positions.
4. Identify when to check for a match versus when to slide the window forward.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. We want to find where the word 'ab' appears as an anagram in the string 'ab'. An anagram means the letters can be rearranged.
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: Is 'ab' an anagram of itself in 'ab'?

content.title: Try a bigger string
content.prompt: Find where 'ab' appears as an anagram in 'cbaebabacd'
content.successMessage: Great! You found matches starting at positions 0 and 6.

content.title: One more challenge
content.prompt: Find where 'abc' appears as an anagram in 'cbaebabacd'
content.successMessage: Well done! You found matches starting at positions 0, 1, and 6.

content.body: What you just did was manually check every possible substring of the longer string to see if it matches the pattern. For each position, you mentally compared character counts. This is the brute force approach.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the string has thousands of characters, checking every possible substring becomes very slow. We need a method that avoids re-scanning the same characters repeatedly. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-checking entire substrings, we can use a lookup structure to remember character frequencies. Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use two frequency maps: one for the pattern (p) and one for the current window in the string (s). As we slide the window, we update the frequency map efficiently by removing the left character and adding the right character.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Example: p='ab', s='cbaebabacd'
1. Create frequency maps for 'ab' and first window 'cb'
2. Slide window: remove 'c', add 'a' → window='ba' (matches!)
3. Continue sliding, updating frequency map each time
4. When window frequency matches pattern frequency, we found an anagram

content.body:
1. Create frequency maps for the pattern string
2. Initialize a frequency map for the first window in the main string
3. Slide the window one character at a time:
   - Remove the leftmost character from the window map
   - Add the new right character to the window map
4. Compare window map with pattern map
5. If they match, record the starting position
6. Repeat until we've checked all possible windows
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create frequency counting function
steps.instruction: Let's start by creating a helper function that builds a frequency map from a string. We'll use an object where keys are characters and values are counts.
steps.hint: Loop through the string and increment counts in an object.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created a frequency counter.

steps.hint: Call createFrequencyMap with the pattern string.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we have our starting window to compare.

steps.title: Slide the window and update
steps.instruction: Implement the sliding window loop. For each new position, update windowFreq by removing the left character and adding the right character.
steps.hint: Use a for loop starting from p.length, update counts, then check if maps are equal.
steps.expectedOutcome: Window should slide and update frequency map correctly
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The window is now sliding efficiently.

steps.title: Complete the implementation
steps.instruction: Finish the function by collecting all starting indices where anagrams are found and return the result array.
steps.hint: After updating windowFreq, check if it matches pFreq and push the starting index.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function should return array of starting indices
steps.feedbackCorrect: Congratulations! You've implemented the complete anagram finder.

steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check each window and collect matching positions.

content.body: Excellent work! You've learned how to find all anagrams in a string using frequency maps and sliding window. Remember: the key insight is to use a lookup structure (frequency map) to remember what we've seen, which lets us compare windows in constant time. This approach transforms an O(n²) brute force solution into an efficient O(n) algorithm.
